transcript.text: Flip a coin. That's your odds of your state legislative race actually being contested in Massachusetts. Since 2014, 51% of races in this state, more than half, have had just one name on the ballot. No opponent, no debate, no choice. Massachusetts ranks dead last in the country for electoral competitiveness. That's not democracy, that's your leaders being chosen for you. And it's not because good candidates don't exist, it's because the system makes it nearly impossible for a challenger to even get on the ballot in the first place. So every 2 years, the same seats go back to the same people and nobody has to explain a single vote. Voters show up to rubber stamp a decision that was already made for them.

transcript.text: In most Massachusetts races, there's no competition. One candidate, one party, no choice. Why does that matter? Think about the only coffee shop in town. If nobody else can open across the street, prices go up and service goes down. Nobody has to try. Politics works the same way. When politicians don't have to compete, they don't have to listen. Since 2014, more than half of the races for the state House and Senate have had just one name on the ballot. Question 3 changes the rules. Every candidate runs in 1 primary and the top 2 finishers face off in November. Two real choices in the fall means every vote has to be earned. That's how you get representatives who actually listen.
